about.title: About Go
about.history.title: History
about.history.p1: Go is one of the oldest strategy board games known, originating in China more than 2500 years ago. There is no exact invention date, historical evidence and traditional legends agree on a very old origin, not a precise year.
about.history.p2: It spread to Korea and, by around the 7th or 8th century, reached Japan. There it became a central part of the culture for centuries, with a weight no other country gave it at the time.
about.history.p3: During the Edo period (17th to 19th centuries), the Tokugawa government funded four official Go schools (Honinbo, Yasui, Inoue, and Hayashi), which competed with each other and professionalized the game long before anything similar existed in other countries.
about.history.p4: In the 20th century Go organized itself more formally (the Nihon Ki-in, Japan's Go association, was founded in 1924) and spread outside East Asia, with federations and tournaments in Europe and the Americas.
about.history.p5: In March 2016, the program AlphaGo (by DeepMind) defeated South Korean professional Lee Sedol, one of the strongest players in the world at the time, four games to one. It was the first time a program beat a top-level professional in a full game, and a surprise even to computer Go researchers, it was expected to take several more years. Hoshi's own bot uses a much simpler version of the same family of techniques as AlphaGo (Monte Carlo tree search), at a far smaller scale.
about.glossary.title: Glossary
about.rules.title: Comparing scoring rules
about.rules.intro: This app uses area scoring (Chinese rules). If you ever play on another platform and see a different result for the same game, that is probably why, not a bug.
about.rules.chinese.title: Area scoring (Chinese rules, the ones this app uses)
about.rules.chinese.description: Each side's score is its own stones left on the board plus the empty points surrounded only by that color. An empty point surrounded by both colors counts for neither. Filling your own territory with a stone does not change the result, since that stone simply counts in place of the empty point it occupied.
about.rules.japanese.title: Territory scoring (Japanese rules)
about.rules.japanese.description: Each side's score is its empty points surrounded only by that color plus the opponent stones captured during the game. Stones left on the board are not counted directly. Unlike area scoring, playing inside your own territory without a need does cost a point, since it turns a territory point into a stone that adds nothing.
about.rules.aga.title: AGA rules (American Go Association)
about.rules.aga.description: Area scoring, like Chinese rules, with an adjustment (a "pass stone") meant to make the result almost always match what Japanese rules would give for the same game.
about.rules.nz.title: New Zealand rules
about.rules.nz.description: Also area scoring, very close to the Chinese version. One of the earliest area-scoring rule sets adopted outside Asia, and a historical reference for several Western clubs and federations.
about.rules.seki.title: Seki (mutual life)
about.rules.seki.description: A position where two rival groups are in contact without either having two eyes, but neither can capture the other: whoever plays first in the shared space would end up with fewer liberties and lose the race. Neither captures, so both groups stay alive as they are. The exact score varies by counting system: in area scoring the stones count as usual, in territory scoring the shared space usually counts as no one's territory.
lesson.n0-l1.title: The board and intersections
lesson.n0-l1.p1: The Go board is a grid of lines. Stones don't go inside the squares, like in chess: they go on the points where lines cross, the intersections.
lesson.n0-l1.p2: A 9x9 board has 81 intersections. To start, this lesson uses a smaller 5x5 board so every point is easy to see.
lesson.n0-l1.demo.step1.prompt: Tap the marked intersection at the center of the board.
lesson.n0-l1.demo.step1.feedback: That's how you play: on the crossing of the lines, never inside a square.
lesson.n0-l1.demo.complete: You know where stones go now. Let's move on to liberties.
lesson.n0-l2.title: Liberties
lesson.n0-l2.p1: Every stone on the board has liberties: the empty points touching it in a straight line (up, down, left, right). Diagonals don't count.
lesson.n0-l2.p2: The black stone in the center has four liberties, one in each direction. Playing next to it, on the opponent's side, removes one.
lesson.n0-l2.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing white. Tap any of the four points next to the black stone.
lesson.n0-l2.demo.step1.feedback: The black stone went from four liberties to three: every enemy stone touching it removes one.
lesson.n0-l2.demo.complete: That's how liberties are counted. Let's move on to groups.
lesson.n0-l3.title: Groups
lesson.n0-l3.p1: Two stones of the same color touching in a straight line form a group, and share all their liberties. If they only touch diagonally, they don't form a group: they stay separate stones, each with its own liberties.
lesson.n0-l3.p2: Connecting stones into a group makes them harder to capture, because the opponent has to fill every liberty of the whole group, not just one stone's.
lesson.n0-l3.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing black. Tap the point next to the black stone to connect and form a group of two.
lesson.n0-l3.demo.step1.feedback: Now it's a single group of two stones, sharing all the liberties left around them.
lesson.n0-l3.demo.complete: That's how groups form. Let's move on to capture.
lesson.n0-l4.title: Capture
lesson.n0-l4.p1: A group with no liberties left cannot stay on the board: it's removed entirely. That's capturing.
lesson.n0-l4.p2: The white stone in the center already has three of its four liberties surrounded. It has one left, below.
lesson.n0-l4.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing black. Tap the point below to take white's last liberty.
lesson.n0-l4.demo.step1.feedback: The white stone ran out of liberties and was removed from the board: it's captured.
lesson.n0-l4.demo.complete: That's how capture works. Let's move on to atari.
lesson.n0-l5.title: Atari
lesson.n0-l5.p1: A group with a single liberty is in atari: one opponent move away from being captured.
lesson.n0-l5.p2: The white group in this example has two liberties, above and below. If black takes one, white is in atari.
lesson.n0-l5.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing black. Tap the point above to put the white group in atari.
lesson.n0-l5.demo.step1.feedback: The white group is down to one liberty: that's atari.
lesson.n0-l5.demo.auto.feedback: White didn't respond to the atari.
lesson.n0-l5.demo.step2.prompt: White didn't respond. Tap the last liberty to capture the group.
lesson.n0-l5.demo.step2.feedback: Captured: if an atari isn't defended, the next move turns it into a capture.
lesson.n0-l5.demo.complete: That's how atari works. Let's move on to suicide.
lesson.n0-l6.title: Suicide
lesson.n0-l6.p1: You can't play a stone that ends up with no liberties, unless that move captures something. That rule is called suicide, and the app won't let you do it.
lesson.n0-l6.p2: The marked point is surrounded by four black stones that aren't in atari. Playing white there wouldn't capture anything.
lesson.n0-l6.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing white. Try playing the marked point, right between the four black stones.
lesson.n0-l6.demo.step1.feedback: The app didn't let you play there: that stone would end up with no liberties and capture nothing, so it's a suicide move, forbidden.
lesson.n0-l6.demo.complete: That's the end of Level 0: you now know the basic rules to play a full game of Atari Go.
lesson.n1-l1.title: The real goal of the game
lesson.n1-l1.p1: The goal of a Go game is simple: by the end, control more points on the board than the opponent, counting your own stones plus the empty territory they surround.
lesson.n1-l1.p2: You don't need to capture everything the opponent has, or fill the whole board. It's enough to have more points than the other player once both agree there's nothing left worth playing.
lesson.n1-l2.title: Passing and the end of the game
lesson.n1-l2.p1: Either player can pass on their turn: place no stone. The game ends when both players pass one right after the other.
lesson.n1-l2.p2: Passing too early can cost points: if there's still a move that changes the result, like an available capture, passing lets it slip by.
lesson.n1-l2.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing black. Instead of passing, tap the white stone in atari to capture it.
lesson.n1-l2.demo.step1.feedback: If you had passed, that white stone would still be on the board. Never pass while there's still a move that changes the result.
lesson.n1-l2.demo.complete: That's how you avoid passing too early. Let's move on to area counting.
lesson.n1-l3.title: Area counting
lesson.n1-l3.p1: Each player's final score is their own stones on the board plus the empty points surrounded only by their color. An empty point touching both colors doesn't count for anyone.
lesson.n1-l3.diagram.caption: In this example both add up to {{score}} points: {{stones}} own stones plus {{territory}} territory each. The middle column doesn't count for anyone: it touches both colors.
lesson.n1-l4.title: Komi
lesson.n1-l4.p1: Black plays first, which gives a real advantage in a game where every point counts. To make up for it, white gets a fixed bonus at the end: komi.
lesson.n1-l4.p2: Hoshi uses a komi of 6.5 points, the standard value for 9x9 boards with area counting. The half point exists so the game never ends in a tie.
lesson.n1-l5.title: Ko
lesson.n1-l5.p1: Ko is a rule that stops you from immediately repeating a previous board position. Without it, two players could capture and recapture the same stone forever.
lesson.n1-l5.p2: If a move would leave the board exactly as it was a few moves back, that move is illegal. You have to play somewhere else first (a ko threat) before you can recapture.
lesson.n1-l5.demo.step1.prompt: Tap the marked point to capture the white stone.
lesson.n1-l5.demo.step1.feedback: Black captured. Notice: if white could recapture right now, the board would go back to exactly how it was before this move.
lesson.n1-l5.demo.step2.prompt: You're playing white. Try recapturing immediately on the point that just emptied out.
lesson.n1-l5.demo.step2.feedback: The app didn't let you: that move would repeat the position from before black's capture. That's how the ko rule works.
lesson.n1-l5.demo.complete: That's how ko works. Let's move on to dead stones.
lesson.n1-l6.title: Dead stones
lesson.n1-l6.p1: A group can be dead without having been captured yet: if it has no way to make two eyes and is fully surrounded, there's nothing it can do to survive, even though the stones are technically still on the board.
lesson.n1-l6.p2: Attacking a group that's already clearly dead doesn't win anything extra. That said, this app doesn't have assisted dead-stone marking at the end of a game yet. Before passing, you have to actually finish the capture, or the area count will treat it as alive.
lesson.n1-l7.title: When to stop playing
lesson.n1-l7.p1: With area counting, your own stone and your own territory point are worth exactly the same. Playing inside your own already-secured territory doesn't add or subtract points directly.
lesson.n1-l7.p2: But it wastes a turn. If there's still a move elsewhere on the board that changes the result, playing inside your own territory is worse than passing: it hands that turn to the opponent.
lesson.n1-l7.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing black. Somewhere on the board there's a white stone in atari: find it and capture it, instead of playing inside your already-sealed territory in the bottom right.
lesson.n1-l7.demo.step1.feedback: Capturing there is worth much more than playing inside your own territory, which wasn't going to add or subtract anything.
lesson.n1-l7.demo.complete: That's the end of Level 1: you now know the full rules to play a real game of Go.
lesson.n2-l1.title: Eye
lesson.n2-l1.p1: An eye is an empty point surrounded only by stones of one color (and, on the edge or corner, by the edge of the board, which counts in the owner's favor).
lesson.n2-l1.diagram.caption: The marked point is an eye: its orthogonal neighbors, and the board edge in this corner, are all black.
lesson.n2-l2.title: Why one eye isn't enough
lesson.n2-l2.p1: As long as a group has other liberties besides the eye, the opponent can't play inside the eye: it would be suicide. But if the eye ends up being the group's last liberty, playing there is no longer suicide, because it captures.
lesson.n2-l2.p2: So a single eye delays death, but doesn't prevent it. You need a second eye so the opponent can never reach that situation.
lesson.n2-l2.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing white. The black group only has that one liberty: tap the marked point to capture it.
lesson.n2-l2.demo.step1.feedback: White could play right in the eye and capture the three black stones: one eye isn't enough if it's the group's last liberty.
lesson.n2-l2.demo.complete: That's why you need more than one eye. Let's move on to two eyes.
lesson.n2-l3.title: Two eyes: unconditional life
lesson.n2-l3.p1: A group with two separate eyes can never die, no matter how many times or how early the opponent moves. To capture it, the opponent would have to play both eyes at once, and that's impossible.
lesson.n2-l3.p2: Playing either eye alone would be suicide for the opponent, because the black group keeps the other eye as a liberty. This is the only absolutely safe kind of life in Go.
lesson.n2-l3.diagram.caption: The two marked empty points are separate eyes of the same black group: unconditional life.
lesson.n2-l4.title: False eye
lesson.n2-l4.p1: It's not enough for the four orthogonal stones to be your color: the diagonals matter too. In the center of the board you need at least three of the four diagonals; on the edge, the two diagonals that exist; in the corner, the single diagonal that exists.
lesson.n2-l4.p2: If a diagonal is missing and that enemy stone can't be captured, the point isn't a real eye: it's a false eye, and sooner or later the group ends up with fewer liberties than it seemed to have.
lesson.n2-l4.diagram.caption: The marked point has its three orthogonal black neighbors, but one of its two edge diagonals is white: that's what makes it a false eye, not a real one.
lesson.n2-l5.title: Eye space
lesson.n2-l5.p1: A space of three empty points in a line, already surrounded by a single group, is neither one eye nor two: it's an eye space. Its fate depends on who plays the middle point first.
lesson.n2-l5.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing black. Tap the middle point of the space to split it into two real eyes.
lesson.n2-l5.demo.step1.feedback: Playing the middle point split the space into two real eyes, one on each side. The group now lives no matter what white does.
lesson.n2-l5.demo.complete: If white had played that same middle point first instead, the group would have died: that's why it's a conditional eye space, it depends on who moves first.
lesson.n2-l6.title: Vital point
lesson.n2-l6.p1: Many life-and-death shapes come down to a single point that decides everything: if the group's owner plays it, the group lives; if the opponent plays it, the group dies. That's the vital point.
lesson.n2-l6.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing white. Tap the marked point to kill the black group.
lesson.n2-l6.demo.step1.feedback: White played the same point that, if black had played it first, would have saved the group. That's why it's called the vital point: it works to live and to kill, depending on who plays it first.
lesson.n2-l6.demo.complete: That's how you recognize a vital point. Let's move on to basic dead shapes.
lesson.n2-l7.title: Basic dead shapes
lesson.n2-l7.p1: These three eye-space shapes show up constantly in real games. They're worth recognizing by heart.
lesson.n2-l7.diagram.rectaDeTres.caption: Straight three: lives if the owner plays the marked center point first, dies if the opponent plays it first.
lesson.n2-l7.diagram.piramide.caption: Pyramid four: just like straight three, it depends on who plays the marked point first, where the three arms meet.
lesson.n2-l7.diagram.cuadrado.caption: Square four: dead no matter who plays first. Not even the owner playing first is enough to live.
lesson.n2-l8.title: Nakade
lesson.n2-l8.p1: Nakade means playing inside an opponent's group's space to reduce it to a single eye, instead of trying to capture it piece by piece from outside.
lesson.n2-l8.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing white. Tap the marked point, inside the black space.
lesson.n2-l8.demo.step1.feedback: That's nakade: playing inside the space to reduce it to a single real eye, even though the whole group is still on the board for now. Since this shape is dead no matter who plays first, nothing else is needed.
lesson.n2-l8.demo.complete: That's the end of Level 2: you now know how to recognize when a group lives or dies.
lesson.n3-l1.title: Double atari
lesson.n3-l1.p1: Sometimes a single move puts two different enemy groups in atari at the same time. The opponent can only respond to one: the other is capturable on the next move.
lesson.n3-l1.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing black. Tap the marked point to put both white groups in atari at once.
lesson.n3-l1.demo.step1.feedback: That move leaves both white groups with a single liberty at the same time: a double atari. White can only save one of the two.
lesson.n3-l1.demo.complete: That's how you recognize a double atari. Let's move on to the ladder.
lesson.n3-l2.title: Ladder (shicho)
lesson.n3-l2.p1: A ladder is a zigzag chase: every time the chaser reduces the fleeing group's liberties to one, that group extends toward its only remaining liberty, and they keep going until the fleeing group runs into the edge of the board without ever getting a third liberty.
lesson.n3-l2.p2: That's why a ladder depends on the whole board, not just the local position: if there's a stone of the fleeing side's color anywhere along the path, the ladder changes completely (next lesson).
lesson.n3-l2.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing white, the chaser. Tap one of the black stone's liberties to reduce them.
lesson.n3-l2.demo.step1.feedback: Black is in atari: it has to extend toward its one remaining liberty.
lesson.n3-l2.demo.auto1.feedback: Black extended toward its only liberty, the only way to stay alive for now.
lesson.n3-l2.demo.step2.prompt: Keep reducing: tap the marked liberty.
lesson.n3-l2.demo.step2.feedback: Black is in atari again, and has to extend again.
lesson.n3-l2.demo.auto2.feedback: Black extended again, but the corner leaves it with less and less room.
lesson.n3-l2.demo.step3.prompt: Last liberty: tap there to capture the whole group.
lesson.n3-l2.demo.step3.feedback: Captured. Black never got a third liberty, so the chase trapped it against the edge.
lesson.n3-l2.demo.complete: That's how you read a ladder. Let's move on to the ladder breaker.
lesson.n3-l3.title: Ladder breaker
lesson.n3-l3.p1: A ladder breaker is a stone of the fleeing side's color, already sitting in the ladder's path before it starts. It changes the result completely, even though the contact position looks identical.
lesson.n3-l3.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing white. This position looks just like the earlier ladder. Try the same reducing move as before.
lesson.n3-l3.demo.step1.feedback: Unlike the earlier ladder, this move doesn't put black in atari: the stone already connected up top-left gives it an extra liberty from the start. Starting this ladder would be a disaster: white would waste moves chasing something that can't be caught.
lesson.n3-l3.demo.complete: That's why it's worth checking for a breaker before starting a ladder. Let's move on to the net.
lesson.n3-l4.title: Net (geta)
lesson.n3-l4.p1: A net (geta) traps a group without chasing it across the whole board like a ladder: a single stone, placed in the right spot, makes any of the opponent's remaining liberties lead right back to atari on the next move.
lesson.n3-l4.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing black. The white stone already has only two liberties. Tap the marked point to set the net.
lesson.n3-l4.demo.step1.feedback: With that stone, white has no way out: wherever it plays among its two liberties, it's back in atari on the next move, without needing to be chased across the board like in a ladder.
lesson.n3-l4.demo.complete: That's how a net works. Let's move on to snapback.
lesson.n3-l5.title: Snapback
lesson.n3-l5.p1: A snapback sacrifices a stone on purpose: it looks like a mistake because the stone is immediately in atari, but when the opponent captures it, their own group ends up with a single liberty, the very point that just opened up.
lesson.n3-l5.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing black. Tap the marked point: your stone will be in atari right away, but it's the correct move.
lesson.n3-l5.demo.step1.feedback: Your stone is down to one liberty. Watch what happens when white captures it.
lesson.n3-l5.demo.auto.feedback: White captured your stone, but had to play right there to do it. Now the whole white group is down to a single liberty: the same point you just freed up.
lesson.n3-l5.demo.step2.feedback: That's a snapback: you sacrificed one stone on purpose to recapture three white stones at once, not just one.
lesson.n3-l5.demo.complete: That's how a snapback works. Let's move on to cutting and connecting.
lesson.n3-l6.title: Cutting and connecting
lesson.n3-l6.p1: Two of your own stones that only touch diagonally aren't a group: they stay separate, sharing a single point that would connect them if either side plays it first. That's a cutting point.
lesson.n3-l6.demo.step1.prompt: You're playing black. Your two stones only touch diagonally. Tap one of the two points that would connect them.
lesson.n3-l6.demo.step1.feedback: Now it's a single group. If you'd left that point and the opponent played it first, your two stones would have been cut apart, each fending for itself.
lesson.n3-l6.demo.complete: That's how you recognize and defend a cutting point. Let's move on to bamboo and tiger's mouth.
lesson.n3-l7.title: Bamboo joint and tiger's mouth
lesson.n3-l7.p1: Some connection shapes can never be cut, so defending them is a wasted move.
lesson.n3-l7.diagram.bamboo.caption: Bamboo joint: the two gaps in the middle connect either way, no matter which one the opponent plays first. If white plays one, black connects through the other. You never need to play there to defend it.
lesson.n3-l7.diagram.tiger.caption: Tiger's mouth: if white played the marked point, its stone would be left with a single liberty. You never need to close that mouth.
lesson.n3-l8.title: Empty triangle
lesson.n3-l8.p1: These three stones form an empty triangle: they occupy three points of a four-point square without needing to, much less efficient than extending toward new space on the board. It's the most common inefficient shape among beginners.
lesson.n3-l8.diagram.caption: The marked point is already effectively covered by the three stones: actually playing it would be redundant, which is why it's worth avoiding this triangle shape in the first place.
lesson.n3-l8.p2: That's the end of Level 3. Level 4 continues on a bigger board (9x13), with the first ideas about shape.
lesson.n4-l1.title: Efficient shape
lesson.n4-l1.p1: Not every shape with the same number of stones is worth the same. These four stones bunched together ("dango") get in each other's way: several of their liberties overlap, so the whole group breathes less than it looks like.
lesson.n4-l1.diagram.dango.caption: Four stones bunched together: only {{libs}} liberties total for the whole group.
lesson.n4-l1.diagram.spread.caption: The same four stones, spread out in knight's-move (keima) jumps without touching: {{libs}} liberties total, double what the bunched shape had.
lesson.n4-l1.p2: Same number of stones, double the breathing room. Spreading stones out instead of bunching them together is the core idea of efficient shape.
lesson.n4-l2.title: The cut in a keima
lesson.n4-l2.p1: A knight's move (keima) connects two stones at a distance, but unlike a solid connection, two real points are left open between them. The opponent can play at either one.
lesson.n4-l2.p2: You're playing white. Touch one of the two points that separate the black stones.
lesson.n4-l2.demo.step1.prompt: Find a point between the two black stones where white can play.
lesson.n4-l2.demo.step1.feedback: The two black stones are no longer directly connected: the top one and the bottom one are now in separate groups. The keima looked like a connection, but it had a real gap to play into.
lesson.n4-l2.demo.complete: That's how you spot the weak point of a keima. On to the hane.
lesson.n4-l3.title: Hane and the risk of a cut
lesson.n4-l3.p1: Wrapping around a stone (hane) gains ground, but it almost always leaves a real cutting point behind. Before you hane, it's worth knowing whether that cut favors you or your opponent.
lesson.n4-l3.p2: You're playing black. Hane around the white stone.
lesson.n4-l3.demo.step1.feedback: You gained ground, but now there's a real cutting point right behind your move.
lesson.n4-l3.demo.auto.feedback: White cut, just as feared. But that cutting stone only has two liberties, both toward the corner.
lesson.n4-l3.demo.step2.prompt: Chase the cutting stone toward the corner.
lesson.n4-l3.demo.step2.feedback: This is the first move of a real ladder: following this same pattern, the cutting stone gets trapped once it reaches the corner, with no liberties left.
lesson.n4-l3.demo.complete: That's how a cut that runs into a ladder gets punished. On to the extension.
lesson.n4-l4.title: Extension from a wall
lesson.n4-l4.p1: A wall isn't worth the same whether you stay glued to it or extend too far away. Extending too short wastes part of the wall's strength; extending too far leaves a real gap the opponent can exploit.
lesson.n4-l4.diagram.short.caption: Short extension: safe, but leaves ground unclaimed in front of the wall. Across full simulated games, this distance consistently came out worse than the balanced extension.
lesson.n4-l4.diagram.balanced.caption: Balanced extension: neither glued to the wall nor too loose. Verified with full simulated games (not by hand): this distance gave the best average result among the ones tested.
lesson.n4-l4.p2: There's no single exact rule that works for every wall, but the idea of aiming for the middle ground, neither too tight nor too loose, held up in the real comparison.
lesson.n4-l5.title: The Big Point Isn't Always the Big Area
lesson.n4-l5.p1: Not all open ground on the board is worth the same. Some of it is already yours in every practical sense: adding a stone there doesn't change anything. Other ground is still undecided, and whoever plays there first gets it. The point that matters most usually isn't the one that looks biggest, it's the one that's still open.
lesson.n4-l5.diagram.secured.caption: Black's corner (top-left) is already sealed. Playing inside it, at the marked point, changes the score by {{delta}} points, verified by counting area before and after: it was already Black's.
lesson.n4-l5.diagram.contested.caption: The smaller-looking pocket on the right still had one open point, marked here. Closing it adds {{delta}} points at once, verified the same way: that ground wasn't settled yet.
lesson.n4-l5.p2: This doesn't mean small areas always beat big ones, it means size on its own doesn't tell you the value of a move. Before comparing two areas, ask which one is still open. That's usually where the real points are.
lesson.n5-l1.title: The Star Point: Two Directions at Once
lesson.n5-l1.p1: A stone on the 4-4 point (hoshi) doesn't commit to one side: it declares interest in two directions at once. That makes it flexible, but it comes at a cost: it doesn't close off any territory by itself, and the 3-3 point remains a weak spot.
lesson.n5-l1.diagram.alone.caption: A single stone on the star point.
lesson.n5-l1.diagram.both.caption: From there, Black can develop downward or to the left: both are natural continuations of the same stone, neither one better than the other by default.
lesson.n5-l1.p2: This flexibility is the star point's strength, but it also explains why it isn't enough on its own to secure the corner: sooner or later, Black has to choose which side to keep developing.
lesson.n5-l2.title: The 3-4 Point Doesn't Decide on Its Own
lesson.n5-l2.p1: A stone on the 3-4 point (komoku) is calm and easy to turn into territory: its main direction runs along one of its two nearby sides. But that direction is only worth as much as the rest of the board on that side.
lesson.n5-l2.diagram.open.caption: Alone on the board, this 3-4 stone wants to develop downward or to the left.
lesson.n5-l2.diagram.blocked.caption: The same stone, but White already has a stone sitting in the path of its main direction (marked). The 3-4 point's natural development downward is already shaped by what's already there.
lesson.n5-l2.p2: That's why playing 3-4 is never an isolated decision: before choosing the point, it's worth checking what's already on the side that stone is going to want to grow toward.
lesson.n5-l3.title: The 3-3 Point: Secure, but With No Side of Its Own
lesson.n5-l3.p1: The 3-3 point is the opposite of the star point: while the 4-4 declares interest in two directions, the 3-3 has none at all. It's the most secure spot in the corner, but a closed world of its own, with no outside influence.
lesson.n5-l3.diagram.star.caption: The star point: from here, Black still has to choose which way to grow.
lesson.n5-l3.diagram.33.caption: The 3-3 point: it's already in the corner, with nothing left to decide about its direction, because it doesn't have one.
lesson.n5-l3.p2: Neither one is better in the abstract: the 3-3 trades flexibility for immediate security. But if your plan depends on that stone later helping out elsewhere on the board, the 3-3 won't give you that.
lesson.n5-l4.title: Corner Enclosure: the Front Door and the Back Door
lesson.n5-l4.p1: After enclosing a corner, there are two directions to keep playing: the primary one (the "front door") and the secondary one (the "back door"). The difference isn't arbitrary: it comes down to what shape the territory ends up with.
lesson.n5-l4.diagram.box.caption: Following the front door (marked) leaves a compact shape, more like a box: the territory grows evenly in two directions.
lesson.n5-l4.diagram.tray.caption: Following the back door (marked) leaves an elongated shape, more like a tray: the territory grows, but narrow and in a single direction.
lesson.n5-l4.p2: A box is worth more than a tray for the same number of stones: that's why the front door is generally the more valuable direction after a corner enclosure.
lesson.n5-l5.title: When Two Stones Point the Same Way
lesson.n5-l5.p1: A stone's direction doesn't get evaluated alone: if another one of your stones already points the same way, the two reinforce each other. Nirensei (two star points on the same side of the board) is the best-known example.
lesson.n5-l5.diagram.aligned.caption: Two star points on the same side: both stones want to develop toward the same stretch of the board, and each one makes the other stronger.
lesson.n5-l5.diagram.opposite.caption: Two star points on opposite sides: each stone pulls toward its own side. Neither one is bad, but they don't reinforce each other the same way.
lesson.n5-l5.p2: Before deciding where to play, ask not just what direction that stone has on its own, but which of your other stones share that same direction.
lesson.n6-l1.title: What a Joseki Is (and Isn't)
lesson.n6-l1.p1: A joseki is a sequence of moves in a corner that theory accepts as roughly balanced for both sides: neither player comes out clearly behind if it's played to the end. But being correct in the abstract isn't the same as being the right move in your actual game. There's a well-known proverb: "memorizing joseki makes you two stones weaker," because copying a sequence without understanding why each move works leaves you stuck the moment your opponent deviates from the book.
lesson.n6-l1.diagram.caption: A typical opening exchange in a corner: Black plays the 4-4 point, White approaches. Together, an exchange like this is what's called a joseki.
lesson.n6-l1.p2: The next lessons aren't a list of sequences to memorize. They're the questions that actually matter: which direction should you block? when is it right to leave a sequence unfinished? why doesn't the 4-4 point secure the corner on its own?
lesson.n6-l2.title: Block Toward Your Own Support
lesson.n6-l2.p1: When your opponent approaches your corner stone, you can almost always block from either side. The question that decides which is better isn't geometric, it's: which side already has something worth reinforcing?
lesson.n6-l2.diagram.support.caption: Black already has a stone further up, on the same side. Blocking toward it (marked) builds a wall that connects toward something that already has value: the block and the support stone work together.
lesson.n6-l2.diagram.empty.caption: The same approach, but blocking the other way (marked): the wall points toward the corner, where Black has nothing else to reinforce. The support stone above stays disconnected from the new wall.
lesson.n6-l2.p2: It's not an absolute rule (sometimes the "empty" side is more urgent for some other reason) but as a starting point, block toward what you already have, not toward what you don't.
lesson.n6-l3.title: Sometimes Not Finishing the Sequence Is Correct
lesson.n6-l3.p1: Tenuki means playing elsewhere on the board instead of responding locally. Every corner sequence, at some point, stops being the biggest move available, and the rest of the board is still waiting.
lesson.n6-l3.diagram.caption: An exchange that's barely started in one corner. The rest of the 13x13 board is still completely empty: is the biggest move really still here?
lesson.n6-l3.p2: The classic proverb is "urgent moves before big moves," but a big point elsewhere also beats continuing a local sequence that's already served its purpose. Ask yourself, on every move: is this still the most urgent thing, or was it two moves ago?
lesson.n6-l4.title: The 4-4 Point Doesn't Secure the Corner Alone
lesson.n6-l4.p1: The 4-4 point (hoshi) trades real territory for speed and influence in both directions at once: unlike the 3-4 point, there's no stone blocking the 3-3 point.
lesson.n6-l4.diagram.alone.caption: A single stone on the 4-4 point. The 3-3 point, in the corner, is still completely open.
lesson.n6-l4.diagram.invasion.caption: White can play directly at 3-3 (marked). Black's 4-4 stone doesn't prevent or punish it by itself: that's why the 3-3 invasion against a 4-4 point is a standard technique, not a random risky move.
lesson.n6-l4.p2: This doesn't mean 4-4 is a bad move: the influence it gives is worth a lot, especially with more stones around it. But playing 4-4 is explicitly choosing influence over immediate safety in that corner.
lesson.n6-l5.title: The Same Joseki, in Any Corner
lesson.n6-l5.p1: A Go board has eight symmetries: rotating or reflecting it changes no rule of the game. If a sequence is correct in one corner, the same sequence, rotated or reflected, is equally correct in any other.
lesson.n6-l5.diagram.original.caption: The block-toward-support shape from the previous lesson, in the bottom-left corner.
lesson.n6-l5.diagram.rotated.caption: The exact same position, rotated 180 degrees by the engine, not redrawn by hand. Same logic, opposite corner.
lesson.n6-l5.p2: When a lesson shows you a shape in one corner of the diagram, don't memorize the coordinates: memorize the relationship between the stones. That relationship is what stays constant, no matter which actual corner of the game it shows up in.
lesson.n7-l1.title: A Moyo Isn't Territory (Yet)
lesson.n7-l1.p1: When several of your stones form a large frame around empty space, that's called a moyo: a zone of influence. It's tempting to count it as points already secured, but it isn't. A moyo's value comes from what it denies the opponent, not from what Black already owns inside it.
lesson.n7-l1.diagram.moyo.caption: Two Black stones on the same side: one in the corner (4-4), one further down (4-10). The space between them and toward the center is a moyo, not territory: there's no White stone inside yet, but there's no sealed point either.
lesson.n7-l1.diagram.invasion.caption: White invades on the third line (marked), halfway between the two Black stones. Count the spaces: a two-space extension toward either side lands in direct contact with a Black stone. There's no room for a comfortable base in there.
lesson.n7-l1.p2: Over time, if White never manages to live or escape, that space does turn into real territory — but that happens later, while Black keeps playing around it, not at the moment the frame goes up.
lesson.n7-l2.title: The Move That Looks Right Here, But Not There
lesson.n7-l2.p1: It's not enough to ask whether a move improves the position where it's played. A move can be locally perfect — the firmest shape, the most uncomfortable contact play — and still be a mistake, if something much bigger is waiting somewhere else on the board.
lesson.n7-l2.diagram.local.caption: White has a lone stone near two Black stones. Pressing it directly (marked) is tempting: it's the single most uncomfortable contact play available against White, right there.
lesson.n7-l2.diagram.global.caption: But the rest of the 19x19 board is still this empty: an entire corner still unclaimed. White's stone is already weak and isn't going anywhere — pressing it now is worth little next to this.
lesson.n7-l2.p2: It's a broader version of the tenuki idea from Level 6: there, the question was whether a sequence was worth finishing. Here the question is more general — before playing the move that looks best in its own corner, check whether that judgment still holds at the scale of the whole board.
lesson.n7-l3.title: Every New Move, In Relation to What's Already There
lesson.n7-l3.p1: Fuseki isn't picking the single biggest point on the board, move after move, without looking at anything else. It's making use of the direction your own stones are already pointing: a stone carries power and direction, and using that well matters as much as the point itself.
lesson.n7-l3.diagram.related.caption: Two Black stones already lined up on the same row. The marked point follows that exact direction: the third move adds its strength to what's already there, instead of starting over.
lesson.n7-l3.diagram.unrelated.caption: This other point is big too — a whole empty corner. But it has no relationship to the two stones above: it doesn't reinforce them or use the direction they're already pointing in. It isn't a bad move by itself, but it leaves three separate groups of stones that don't help each other, instead of two that do.
lesson.n7-l3.p2: On a 19x19 board this matters even more than on smaller ones: there's more than enough room to play big, isolated points all game long without any stone ever helping another.
lesson.n7-l4.title: A Moyo Doesn't Need Defending Point by Point
lesson.n7-l4.p1: When the opponent invades your framework, the instinct is to rush in and capture it right away. But a moyo doesn't need to be defended intersection by intersection: while the opponent tries to live or escape in there, every move you make around it keeps adding pressure and, over time, real territory.
lesson.n7-l4.diagram.caption: The same invasion from the previous lesson. Black doesn't have to resolve it immediately: play can continue around it, letting White's room to live shrink on its own, move by move.
lesson.n7-l4.p2: Being patient isn't the same as giving up. It's continuing to play with a plan, letting the balance of strength do the work, instead of spending an extra move just to feel safe.
lesson.n7-l5.title: Direction Tells You Where to Look, Not What to Do There
lesson.n7-l5.p1: Everything in this level — moyo, whole-board judgment, playing in relation to what's already there, patience — helps you decide which part of the board deserves attention. It doesn't replace reading: once stones come into contact, you have to calculate the actual sequence, not just rely on a sense of direction.
lesson.n7-l5.diagram.caption: Just two stones in direct contact. The question has already changed: it's no longer where to play, it's what actually happens if this fight is followed to the end.
lesson.n7-l5.p2: No principle in this level fights a battle for you. It gets you to the right fight, in the right part of the board — the rest is still reading.
lesson.n8-l1.title: An Attack Has to Build Something Too
lesson.n8-l1.p1: Chasing a weak group isn't a plan by itself. A good attack leaves something behind when it's over — territory, influence, a wall facing somewhere useful — instead of settling for the simple joy of the chase.
lesson.n8-l1.diagram.caption: Two weak White stones, surrounded from two sides. Black's stones don't just shrink White's space: the outward-facing side of those same Black stones looks toward the entire top-left corner, still empty. Attacking this way leaves something built, whatever happens to the White group.
lesson.n8-l1.p2: If those same attacking stones instead faced an area where Black already had everything secured, the pressure on White would be exactly the same — but nothing new would be left standing once the fight ended.
lesson.n8-l2.title: Attack With What's Already There
lesson.n8-l2.p1: The most effective way to attack isn't the most aggressive move available: it's the one that makes use of a stone you already had in place, instead of starting a fresh attack from nothing.
lesson.n8-l2.diagram.supported.caption: Black already had a stone on the left side. The marked move doesn't attack alone: it leans on that stone, and together they take away far more space than White can use.
lesson.n8-l2.diagram.isolated.caption: The same pressure on White, but played from the other side, far from the stone Black already had. A brand-new attack, alone, that makes no use of anything already built.
lesson.n8-l2.p2: Before choosing which side to attack from, check which of your own stones are already nearby: the difference between the two moves above doesn't show up on the White group — it shows up in what Black has left afterward.
lesson.n8-l3.title: You Can't Fight Hard Here If You're Weak There
lesson.n8-l3.p1: Common sense says that if you have a weak position in one place, you can't fight strongly somewhere else. Starting a new fight while a group of your own is still unresolved splits your attention between two fronts — and in a real fight, that costs you.
lesson.n8-l3.diagram.caption: Black's corner group still isn't settled: two loose stones, not yet connected or alive. Meanwhile, on the other side of the board, Black and White are already in direct contact — a new fight starting just as the corner still needs attention.
lesson.n8-l3.p2: This doesn't mean you can never fight while something elsewhere is weak — sometimes there's no choice. It means knowing you're fighting at a disadvantage, and settling your own weakness as soon as the fight allows it.
lesson.n8-l4.title: Not Every Group Is Worth the Same
lesson.n8-l4.p1: In the middle of a big fight, trying to save every one of your groups at once usually costs too much. You have to adapt to the whole board: sacrifice what should be sacrificed, and keep what's actually worth keeping.
lesson.n8-l4.diagram.caption: The small group in the corner, boxed in with little room to grow, against the diagonal in the center, which still faces the entire open board. If you have to choose where to fight, they're not worth the same.
lesson.n8-l4.p2: This isn't the same as giving up easily: it's recognizing, move by move, which fight is worth having and which is worth letting go before spending more stones on it.
lesson.n8-l5.title: If You're Already Ahead on Points, Don't Go Looking for a Fight
lesson.n8-l5.p1: Not every advantage looks the same. Sometimes one player already has points secured on the board, while the other has, instead, a wall of strength facing the center, with no territory yet. If you're already ahead on points, walking into a fight exactly where your opponent is strong is a risk you don't need to take.
lesson.n8-l5.diagram.caption: Black has already settled two corners, each with a supporting stone. White has no territory yet, but has this diagonal wall facing the center: strength for fighting, not points. Black doesn't need to go in there looking for more — Black is already ahead.
lesson.n8-l5.p2: In this case, the fight favors White more than Black: it's where White is strong. When you're already ahead, the safe move is almost always worth more than the ambitious one.
concept.LIBERTADES.label: Liberties
concept.LIBERTADES.summary: The empty points next to a stone or group.
concept.CAPTURA_SIMPLE.label: Simple capture
concept.CAPTURA_SIMPLE.summary: A group with no liberties left is removed from the board.
concept.ATARI_IGNORADO.label: Ignored atari
concept.ATARI_IGNORADO.summary: A group with one liberty was not defended and got captured.
concept.AUTOATARI.label: Self-atari
concept.AUTOATARI.summary: A move leaves your own group with only one liberty for no gain.
concept.CAPTURA_PERDIDA.label: Missed capture
concept.CAPTURA_PERDIDA.summary: A legal capturing move was available and was not played.
concept.KO.label: Ko
concept.KO.summary: The rule that forbids immediately repeating a previous board position.
concept.CONTEO_AREA.label: Area counting
concept.CONTEO_AREA.summary: Your score is your own stones on the board plus the points they surround.
concept.RELLENO_TERRITORIO_PROPIO.label: Filling your own territory
concept.RELLENO_TERRITORIO_PROPIO.summar: Playing inside your own secure territory loses a point for nothing.
concept.PASE_PREMATURO.label: Premature pass
concept.PASE_PREMATURO.summary: Passing while a move could still change the result by a meaningful margin.
concept.PIEDRA_MUERTA_ATACADA_EN_VANO.su: Spending moves capturing a stone that was already dead and worthless to attack.
concept.DOS_OJOS.label: Two eyes
concept.DOS_OJOS.summary: A group with two separate eyes can never be captured.
concept.OJO_FALSO.label: False eye
concept.OJO_FALSO.summary: An eye-like point that can still be captured because of its diagonals.
concept.RELLENO_OJO_PROPIO.label: Filling your own eye
concept.RELLENO_OJO_PROPIO.summary: Playing inside your own simple eye for no reason, without capturing anything.
concept.PUNTO_VITAL.label: Vital point
concept.PUNTO_VITAL.summary: The single point that decides whether a group lives or dies.
concept.NAKADE.label: Nakade
concept.NAKADE.summary: Playing inside a group's space to reduce it to a single eye.
concept.GRUPO_MURIO_SIN_OJOS.label: Group died without eyes
concept.GRUPO_MURIO_SIN_OJOS.summary: A group of four or more stones died without ever having two eyes.
concept.DOBLE_ATARI.label: Double atari
concept.DOBLE_ATARI.summary: One move puts two separate groups in atari at the same time.
concept.ESCALERA.label: Ladder
concept.ESCALERA.summary: A chase across the board that captures a fleeing group, unless it hits a breaker stone.
concept.ESCALERA_FALLIDA.label: Failed ladder
concept.ESCALERA_FALLIDA.summary: Starting a ladder that does not work because a breaker stone is already on the board.
concept.RED_GETA.label: Net
concept.RED_GETA.summary: A capture that traps a stone without needing to read a long chase.
concept.SNAPBACK.label: Snapback
concept.SNAPBACK.summary: Sacrificing a stone on purpose in order to recapture right after.
concept.CORTE_NO_DEFENDIDO.label: Undefended cut
concept.CORTE_NO_DEFENDIDO.summary: A cutting point was left without defense and the opponent cut through it.
concept.CONEXION_INNECESARIA.label: Unnecessary connection
concept.CONEXION_INNECESARIA.summary: Defending a connection that could not have been cut in the first place.
concept.TRIANGULO_VACIO.label: Empty triangle
concept.TRIANGULO_VACIO.summary: The most common inefficient shape among beginners.
concept.PRIMERA_LINEA_TEMPRANA.label: Early first line
concept.PRIMERA_LINEA_TEMPRANA.summary: Playing on the board's edge line early in the game, with no fight nearby.
concept.JUGADA_LEJOS_DEL_COMBATE.label: Move far from the fight
concept.JUGADA_LEJOS_DEL_COMBATE.summary: Playing somewhere quiet while a group nearby still needs urgent attention.
concept.FORMA_EFICIENTE.label: Efficient shape
concept.FORMA_EFICIENTE.summary: Spreading stones out instead of bunching them together: the same number of stones breathes far more.
concept.CORTE_DEL_KEIMA.label: Keima cut
concept.CORTE_DEL_KEIMA.summary: The knight's move isn't a solid connection: it leaves real points where the opponent can cut.
concept.HANE_Y_CORTE.label: Hane and the cut
concept.HANE_Y_CORTE.summary: Wrapping around a stone gains ground but almost always leaves a real cutting point behind.
concept.EXTENSION_DESDE_PARED.label: Extension from a wall
concept.EXTENSION_DESDE_PARED.summary: Neither glued to the wall nor too loose: some extension distances are more balanced than others.
concept.DIRECCION_LADO_GRANDE.label: Reading the Bigger Point
concept.DIRECCION_LADO_GRANDE.summary: A framework that looks big can already be settled; a small-looking gap can still be the real point.
concept.PUNTO_ESTRELLA_DOS_DIRECCIONES.s: A 4-4 stone declares interest in two sides at once, in exchange for not closing off territory.
concept.PUNTO_3_4_DEPENDE_ESQUINAS.label: 3-4 Depends on the Other Corners
concept.PUNTO_3_4_DEPENDE_ESQUINAS.summa: A 3-4 point's main direction is only worth as much as the rest of the board on that side.
concept.PUNTO_3_3_SIN_DIRECCION.label: 3-3 Has No Direction
concept.PUNTO_3_3_SIN_DIRECCION.summary: The safest point in the corner, but a closed world with no outside influence.
concept.PUERTA_PRINCIPAL_TRASERA.label: Front Door and Back Door
concept.PUERTA_PRINCIPAL_TRASERA.summary: After a corner enclosure, the primary direction usually leaves a more compact shape than the secondary one.
concept.COMBINAR_DIRECCIONES.label: Combining Directions
concept.COMBINAR_DIRECCIONES.summary: Two stones pointing toward the same side of the board reinforce each other, as in nirensei.
concept.QUE_ES_JOSEKI.label: What a Joseki Is
concept.QUE_ES_JOSEKI.summary: A locally balanced sequence, not a memorized answer that works in any context.
concept.BLOQUEO_HACIA_APOYO.label: Block Toward Support
concept.BLOQUEO_HACIA_APOYO.summary: Facing an approach, blocking toward a friendly stone is usually worth more than blocking toward empty space.
concept.TENUKI_JOSEKI.label: Tenuki
concept.TENUKI_JOSEKI.summary: Leaving a local sequence unfinished because a bigger move has appeared elsewhere.
concept.HOSHI_INVASION_3_3.label: 4-4 and the 3-3 Invasion
concept.HOSHI_INVASION_3_3.summary: The 4-4 point favors influence over territory: the 3-3 point stays open for the opponent.
concept.JOSEKI_SIMETRIA.label: Joseki Symmetry
concept.JOSEKI_SIMETRIA.summary: The same sequence, rotated or reflected, is equally correct in any corner of the board.
concept.MOYO_NO_ES_TERRITORIO.label: Moyo, Not Territory
concept.MOYO_NO_ES_TERRITORIO.summary: A framework of influence denies the opponent a base; it isn't secured points yet.
concept.JUICIO_LOCAL_VS_GLOBAL.label: Local vs. Global Judgment
concept.JUICIO_LOCAL_VS_GLOBAL.summary: A locally perfect move can still be a mistake if it ignores something bigger elsewhere on the board.
concept.RELACION_CON_PIEDRAS_PROPIAS.sum: A move is worth more when it makes use of the direction your stones are already pointing.
concept.PACIENCIA_Y_MARGEN.label: Patience and Room to Grow
concept.PACIENCIA_Y_MARGEN.summary: A moyo doesn't need point-by-point defense: pressure from around it is enough, given time.
concept.DIRECCION_NO_ES_TODO.label: Direction Isn't Everything
concept.DIRECCION_NO_ES_TODO.summary: A sense of direction picks where to fight; reading the actual sequence out is still necessary.
concept.ATACAR_CONSTRUYENDO.label: Attacking While Building
concept.ATACAR_CONSTRUYENDO.summary: A good attack leaves territory or influence behind, not just a chased weak group.
concept.USAR_PIEDRAS_PROPIAS_PARA_ATACAR: The most effective attack makes use of a stone already in place, not a new isolated one.
concept.NO_PELEAR_CON_DEBILIDAD.label: Don't Fight From Weakness
concept.NO_PELEAR_CON_DEBILIDAD.summary: You can't fight strongly on one side while a group of your own is still weak on another.
concept.SACRIFICAR_LO_NECESARIO.label: Sacrifice What Should Be Sacrificed
concept.SACRIFICAR_LO_NECESARIO.summary: In a big fight, trying to save every group at once usually costs more than it's worth.
concept.NO_PELEAR_SIN_NECESIDAD.label: Don't Fight Without a Reason
concept.NO_PELEAR_SIN_NECESIDAD.summary: If you're already ahead on points, fighting where your opponent is strong is a risk you don't need.
